newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Casio's profits surge on digital watch sales.
newsitem.headline: Japan Casio's profits surge on digital watch sales.

text.p: Japan's watch and calculator giant Casio Computer Co Ltd on Tuesday unveiled a sharp rise in its earnings last business year, boosted by strong sales of its digital watches and the yen's steep fall.
Casio also made a stronger earnings forecast for the current business year to March 1998, based on its aggressive project to manufacture new products with additional value.

"Profitability in the watch business soared, as G-shock became a well-known brand worldwide that pushed up sales in digital watches overall," Casio said in a statement. G-Shock is a sturdy type of watch that has become popular with young consumers.

Casio said its group net profit surged a surprising 432.4 percent to 3.7 billion yen ($32.7 million) in the business year to March 31, 1997, up from an actual profit of 695 million yen ($6.15 million) a year earlier.
For 1997/98, the company forecast that its group net profit would rally further to 6.5 billion yen ($57.5 million).
The strong earnings and a bullish forecast had been mostly factored into the share price. On the Tokyo bourse, the shares gained 18 yen to close the Tuesday session at 908 yen.
Casio also said that sales in digital cameras rose sharply, helped by its new products, while sales of hand-held personal computers had risen in the United States since their launch in last November.
The firm its sales of personal handy phones also increased. Personal handy phones are type of cellular phone developed in Japan that are simpler and cheaper than conventional mobile phones.
The series of new products lifted the company's sales on overseas markets in particular by 17.7 percent to 149 billion yen ($1.31 billion), the company said.

On a parent basis, the strong sales boosted Casio's current profit by 70.2 percent to 10.49 billion yen ($92.8 million) last business year, but its net profit rose only 17.8 percent to 4.22 billion yen ($37.3 million) due to losses resulted from appraisal losses in its subsidiaries' stocks, the company said.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses on non-operating activities such as investments in stocks. ($1=113 yen)
